wine.name: Sigalas Kavalieros
wine.grapes: Assyrtiko alone, from vines of sixty years and more growing on their own roots.
wine.sites: Kavalieros, a single high block in the village of Imerovigli, where the old vines grow in the island's volcanic ash and pumice, woven low into kouloura baskets against the wind and to hold the night's moisture.
wine.making: The juice is fermented in stainless steel tanks at a controlled temperature. The wine then rests on its fine lees in tank for about eighteen months, stirred often in the first months and less as time passes, and it never sees oak before bottling.
wine.glass: Ripe lemon, lemon verbena and orange blossom over chalk and a strong vein of salt; creamy and full in the mouth, yet held taut by high acidity to a long, saline close.
wine.ageing: Open enough to enjoy on release, it is built to keep, and the house expects it to last ten years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with a few minutes in the glass; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The island's Protected Designation of Origin for dry white wine of at least 85 per cent Assyrtiko.
The name of the single vineyard block at Imerovigli that gives the wine.

records.table: Kavalieros is Domaine Sigalas's single vineyard Assyrtiko from one high block at Imerovigli, old vines woven into baskets in volcanic ash. Eighteen months on its lees in steel give it a creamy weight around the salt and lemon, so pour it with grilled fish.
records.story: The founder came from a Santorini family that, like most on the island, grew vines, and he spent the summers of his boyhood there before he trained as a mathematician, as the house tells it. In 1991 he bottled his first wine, a dry Santorini, at Oia in the north of the island, and the estate grew up among the vineyards of the plain there, working Assyrtiko on its own roots, since phylloxera never took hold in the ash. Beside the estate's Santorini came wines of single places, and Kavalieros was drawn from one high block of vines more than sixty years old in the village of Imerovigli. Bottled apart and given a long rest on its lees in steel rather than time in oak, it lets the site speak without wood. After a Greek investor bought a majority of the estate, its running passed in January 2020 to Kir-Yianni, the wine company of Naoussa in the north of mainland Greece, and in 2025 Kir-Yianni bought that majority itself. To a sommelier, Kavalieros is the bottle for a guest who wants to taste one named Santorini vineyard rather than a blend from many villages.

others.name: Sigalas Santorini
others.note: The estate's dry Santorini of Assyrtiko, the wine it first bottled in 1991.

traps: Domaine Sigalas has its cellar at Oia, but Kavalieros grows in another village, Imerovigli, so the wine is not a wine of Oia.
Kavalieros sees no oak: its creamy weight comes from about eighteen months on its fine lees in steel tanks.

wine.name: Estate Argyros Cuvée Monsignori
wine.sites: The Monsignori parcel at Episkopi Gonia, where Assyrtiko grows on its own roots, low in the island's volcanic ash and pumice, from vines the estate dates to more than two hundred years.
wine.making: The juice is fermented in temperature controlled stainless steel tanks, and the wine is then raised in tank on its fine lees for most of a year, about eleven months for the 2022 vintage, with no oak before bottling.
wine.glass: White peach, lemon curd and beeswax over brine and wet stone; broad, dense and strong in alcohol, yet carried by firm acidity to a long, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Broad enough to enjoy within a year or two of release, it is made to keep, and the estate expects it to age for more than ten years.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, not colder, so that its weight shows; no need to decant; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The name of the old vine parcel at Episkopi Gonia the wine is drawn from.
The island's Protected Designation of Origin for dry white wine led by Assyrtiko.

records.table: Cuvée Monsignori is Estate Argyros's old vine Assyrtiko from one parcel at Episkopi Gonia, where ungrafted vines are counted in centuries. Raised on its lees in steel without oak, it is broad, waxy and salty, a white to pour with grilled octopus or lobster.
records.story: The Argyros family has tended vines on Santorini since the eighteenth century, by its own account, and the estate dates itself to 1903, when its founder began making wine under the family's name at Episkopi Gonia. Its vineyards hold old vines on their own roots, many never replanted, since phylloxera could not live in the island's volcanic soil. In 1974 a new head of the family took over, and the estate's standing rose under him, as the estate's own history and other accounts have it. The fourth generation followed, and in the 2010s the estate moved into a new winery that keeps the old cellars and the press of 1903 beside it. Cuvée Monsignori comes from the parcel of that name at Episkopi, from vines the estate dates to more than two centuries, made as a white of one place and raised on its lees without oak. From the harvest of 2021 the estate released no Monsignori at all, by its own announcement, and the cuvée returned with the next vintage. For a sommelier, Monsignori is the glass that shows what vines two centuries old give on Santorini: weight, wax and salt.

others.name: Estate Argyros Assyrtiko
others.note: The estate's dry Santorini, fermented in steel and kept a few months on its fine lees.

traps: Monsignori is the name of a parcel, not a rank: the wine carries no classification beyond the Santorini appellation.
Santorini's vines grow ungrafted because phylloxera cannot live in the volcanic ash, not because of any quarantine.

wine.name: Gaia Thalassitis
wine.sites: Old vines, close to eighty years by the house's count, in the villages of Episkopi, Akrotiri and Pyrgos, on the island's volcanic ash and pumice, with yields kept low.
wine.making: The grapes spend half a day chilled on their skins before pressing, and the juice is fermented cool, at about 16 to 17 degrees Celsius, in stainless steel tanks. The wine is then kept in steel, untouched by oak, until bottling.
wine.glass: Lime zest, grapefruit and lemon over meadow herbs and a faint note of tobacco; dry and taut, with high, cutting acidity and a long, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and ready on release; the house suggests two to three years in the cellar, which soften its edge as honey and riper fruit come through.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of middling size.

label.means: The wine's name, which the house takes from an ancient Greek habit of mixing wine with sea water.
The island's Protected Designation of Origin for dry white wine of at least 85 per cent Assyrtiko.

records.table: Thalassitis was Gaia's first wine, a Santorini Assyrtiko from old vines in three villages, fermented cool and kept in steel with no oak. Taut, lemony and salty, it is the island's plain style: pour it cold with oysters, grilled fish or feta.
records.story: Two agronomists founded Gaia in 1994, and its first wine was Thalassitis, a dry Santorini of Assyrtiko, as the house tells it. They named it, the house says, after an ancient Greek habit of mixing wine with sea water, which old texts describe in some detail. The Santorini winery took over a stone tomato factory built early in the twentieth century on the beach at Exo Gonia, on the island's east coast, which had made purée from the island's small tomatoes until it closed in the 1970s. In 1997 the partners built a second winery among their own vineyards at Koutsi in Nemea, on the Peloponnese, for Agiorgitiko, so that one house speaks for both the island and the mainland. On Santorini they went on to ferment Assyrtiko with its own yeasts in steel, oak and acacia, and from 2009 they lowered bottles of Thalassitis into the sea off the island to age, an echo of the name. Thalassitis itself stayed the plain style, fermented cool and kept from wood. For a sommelier, it is the bottle that teaches what Santorini Assyrtiko tastes like before oak or long lees change it.

others.name: Assyrtiko by Gaia Wild Ferment
others.note: Santorini Assyrtiko fermented with its own yeasts in steel tanks and in French oak, American oak and acacia barrels.

others.name: Gaia Estate

Gaia makes wine in two appellations, Santorini for Assyrtiko and Nemea for Agiorgitiko, so read the label for the origin.
Thalassitis Submerged is the same wine aged under the sea, not another grape and not a sweet wine.

report: Searches for this record: seven of the group's 35, three restricted to gaiawines.gr or winesofgreece.org; no fetch tried on it. The winery at Exo Gonia, on the east coast between Kamari and Monolithos, is the house's Santorini and visit pages with the Wines of Greece winery page beside them.

The plan's why calls Thalassitis the sea stone; no source gave that meaning and the house's pages give no gloss. Two trade pieces (The Shout, Grape Collective) say the name comes from an ancient Greek habit of mixing wine with sea water, which the record tells as the house's account; the plan's why may want rewording.
The two founders are living and never named: people.json lists one, and the other, Leon Karatsalos, should be added.

The making rests on the importer's sheet (steel, twelve hours chilled on the skins) and a merchant's notes (16 to 17 degrees Celsius); a merchant's four months on the lees for one vintage is left out for want of a second source.

The sea cellar's depth (thirty metres at first, twenty later) and the first year's losses each rest on one source and are left out; the start in 2009 rests on The Shout and the Wine With Seth encyclopaedia.
The rename of the old oak fermented Thalassitis as Nykteri is the house's own page; the library's Thalassitis Submerged as a deliberate provocation is not repeated.

wine.name: Hatzidakis Nykteri
wine.sites: Vineyards at Megalochori, old Assyrtiko vines growing on their own roots in the island's volcanic soil.
wine.making: Overripe grapes, picked by hand, are chilled overnight, destemmed and left twelve hours on their skins. The juice ferments with its own yeasts at 17 to 18 degrees Celsius, and the wine matures about twelve months in French oak barrels of several sizes before it is bottled unfiltered.
wine.glass: Baked apple, preserved lemon and toasted almond over honey, smoke and a breath of sea air; golden, full and broad, with Assyrtiko's acidity keeping the weight fresh.
wine.ageing: Tight and closed when young, it opens over several years in bottle, and the house gives it more than ten years.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle if it seems closed; a large white wine glass.

label.means: Night work: a dry Santorini of at least 13.5 per cent alcohol, aged at least three months in oak.
The island's Protected Designation of Origin, within which Nykteri is a named style.

records.table: Hatzidakis Nykteri is old vine Assyrtiko from Megalochori, picked overripe, fermented with its own yeasts and aged a year in French oak: the riper, oaked style of Santorini, named for the night pressing. Broad and nutty with a salty spine, it suits lobster or roast pork.
records.story: Nykteri means night work: grapes picked for it were pressed during the night after the harvest, and the name came to mean a riper dry wine of Santorini, aged in oak, by the account of the national wine body. The house began with an oenologist born on Crete, who came to the island in 1991 as chief oenologist of the Boutari winery there, and his wife, who ran that winery's hospitality. Her family's vineyard at Pyrgos, abandoned since her parents left the island after the earthquake of 1956, became their own, and in a cave at its end he made a small cellar. The first bottles, a dry Santorini and a red Mavrotragano of the 1997 vintage, were released in 1998. The house farmed its vineyard organically and had it certified. In 2000 it bought a vineyard above a larger cave for its Vinsanto, and in 2016 it moved to a cellar on the road from Pyrgos to Emporio. The founder died in 2017, and his family took the house on. For a sommelier, its Nykteri is the bottle that shows a guest Santorini can be rich and oaked and yet taste of salt.

report: Searches for this record: five of the group's 35, two restricted to hatzidakiswines.gr; no fetch tried on it.
The founder, Haridimos Hatzidakis, died in August 2017 in two accounts (one says May 2017, one 2016); his year of birth was found in none, so he is described, not named, and the house keeps its name.

His widow, who founded the house with him, and their eldest daughter, who directs it, are living and never named; Konstantina Chryssou and Stella Hatzidaki are not yet in people.json and should be added.
Founded 1997 rests on the house's own pages (a cave winery since 1997, first bottles of the 1997 vintage released in 1998); one critic's site gives 1996 and one merchant 1999 for the first bottles.

The plan's why says the founder revived the island's Nykteri; no source said so and the record does not. The house's claim that its vineyard was the first on Santorini certified organic rests on the house alone and is left out; the story says only that it was farmed organically and certified.

Organic farming for the Nykteri's own vineyards is said by one merchant and denied by another for a recent vintage, so the wine fields leave it out; the vineyards at Megalochori are the house's page with two merchants beside it.
The pick stands: the house's dry Santorinis are as well known, but Nykteri is the wine of the style the plan asks to teach, and the house names it on its own page.

wine.name: Santo Vinsanto
wine.grapes: Assyrtiko, the great majority, with Aidani.
wine.sites: Grapes from the union's member growers across the island, own rooted vines in the volcanic ash and pumice of Santorini.
wine.making: Picked in August, the grapes are laid in the sun to dry for about a week to ten days, then fermented slowly over six to eight weeks. The wine is aged for years in oak barrels before bottling, three years in small barrels for the 2020 vintage.
wine.glass: Dried apricot, raisin and fig over cinnamon, clove and caramel; deep amber, thick and sweet, yet cut by a fine thread of acidity that keeps it from cloying.
wine.ageing: Ready on release and long lived; the union has released vintages after more than twenty years in oak, darker and turned towards coffee and dates.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small dessert wine glass, poured in small measures.

label.means: Santorini's sweet wine of sun dried grapes, at least 51 per cent Assyrtiko, aged at least two years.
The island's Protected Designation of Origin, which covers the sweet Vinsanto as well as the dry whites.

records.table: Santo Vinsanto is the sweet wine of Santorini's growers' union: Assyrtiko and Aidani dried in the sun for a week or more, fermented slowly and aged years in oak. Apricot, raisin and cinnamon ride on bright acidity, so serve it cool, in small glasses, after dinner.
records.story: Santo Wines began in 1911 as the Santorini Vine and Wine Protection Fund, by its own account, set up for the island's growers. In 1947 it became the Union of Santorini Cooperatives, formed to process, export and promote the island's produce, above all its wine. Its members are the island's smallholders, whose grapes it takes in and makes into dry whites and the sweet Vinsanto. In 1992 the union completed a new winery in the village of Pyrgos. For Vinsanto, the sweet wine of grapes dried in the sun after the August harvest, the turning point came in 2002, when, as the union's timeline and other accounts record, a European ruling reserved the name Vinsanto for the sweet wine of Santorini, while Italy kept vin santo for its own. The union's Vinsanto carries its vintage and spends years in oak, and older bottlings are held for a decade or two more before release. For a sommelier, Santo's Vinsanto is the ready answer when a guest asks for Santorini's sweet wine, and the bottle that shows it is never fortified.

others.name: Santo Vinsanto 12 Years Ageing
others.note: The same sun dried wine held at least twelve years in French oak barrels before bottling.

others.name: Santo Wines Santorini
others.note: The union's dry white of Assyrtiko under the Santorini appellation.

traps: Santorini Vinsanto, one word, is sun dried Assyrtiko from the island; Tuscan Vin Santo, two words, is made from other grapes dried indoors.
Vinsanto is sweet because its grapes are dried in the sun before fermenting; it is never fortified with grape spirit.
Santo Wines is the island's union of cooperatives, not a family estate.

Nykteri

report: Searches for this record: three of the group's 35, two restricted to santowines.gr, with one of Wikipedia for 1947 and 2002; the appellation's rules are the Wines of Greece page, read for the whole group in two more searches.
The union dates itself to 1911 in its first form; founded keeps the plan's and the region record's 1947, the year it became the Union, in the union's own timeline and Wikipedia.

The fact sheets differ by vintage on drying (six to eight days, eight to ten) and on time in oak (three years in small barrels for one vintage, six in another passage), so the record says a week to ten days and years in oak.
The grape shares (about 85 per cent Assyrtiko, 15 Aidani) are one vintage's sheet and are told as the great majority.
The Venetian and Ottoman history of Vinsanto and the story of the name rest on Wikipedia alone and are left out; so the story tells no history of the wine before the ruling of 2002.
